chief_complaint: chronic painless foul-smelling ear drainage for months, progressive hearing loss, and pearly white keratin mass in attic of eardrum
hpi_details: 45M with lifelong ear infections presenting with fetid otorrhea and conductive hearing loss where otoscopy reveals a pearly white keratinaceous sac retracting into the pars flaccida (superior tympanic membrane) with bony scutum erosion requiring surgical tympanomastoidectomy.
ideas: worried this chronic ear drainage might mean something serious is eroding the bone in his ear
concerns: worried the constant foul-smelling drainage means something is seriously wrong and that he's losing his hearing permanently
expectations: wants a clear diagnosis and to understand whether surgery is really necessary

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Cholesteatoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes definitive surgical excision via tympanomastoidectomy, since cholesteatoma will not resolve with antibiotics alone and can progressively erode surrounding bone, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic painless foul-smelling ear drainage for months, progressive hearing loss, and pearly white keratin mass in attic of eardrum

Key HPI features: 45M with lifelong ear infections presenting with fetid otorrhea and conductive hearing loss where otoscopy reveals a pearly white keratinaceous sac retracting into the pars flaccida (superior tympanic membrane) with bony scutum erosion requiring surgical tympanomastoidectomy.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 76, BP 128/82, afebrile. Otoscopic examination reveals a pearly white keratin debris-filled retraction pocket in the pars flaccida (attic) of the tympanic membrane, with erosion of the adjacent bony scutum. Foul-smelling, painless otorrhea noted on removal of debris. Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear; Rinne test reveals bone conduction greater than air conduction, confirming conductive hearing loss. No nystagmus, facial weakness, or mastoid tenderness.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Cholesteatoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chronic otitis externa without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dizziness, facial weakness, or severe headache — could indicate erosion into the inner ear or intracranial spread.
management_principles: Definitive surgical management: refer to Otolaryngology for Tympanomastoidectomy (canal wall up or canal wall down technique) to completely excise the cholesteatoma matrix and prevent recurrence or further bony erosion
Preoperative High-Resolution CT of the temporal bone to map the extent of bony erosion (ossicular chain, tegmen tympani, lateral semicircular canal, facial nerve canal) and screen for complications
Initiate topical antibiotic ear drops (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) and regular aural toilet to control active infection and reduce mucosal edema preoperatively
Arrange long-term post-operative surveillance (otoscopy plus non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI) for recurrent or residual cholesteatoma
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 45M with a history of lifelong ear infections presenting with months of painless, foul-smelling otorrhea and progressive conductive hearing loss, with otoscopic findings concerning for cholesteatoma.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 76, BP 128/82, afebrile. Otoscopic examination reveals a pearly white keratin debris-filled retraction pocket in the pars flaccida (attic) of the tympanic membrane, with erosion of the adjacent bony scutum. Foul-smelling, painless otorrhea noted on removal of debris. Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear; Rinne test reveals bone conduction greater than air conduction, confirming conductive hearing loss. No nystagmus, facial weakness, or mastoid tenderness.
reference_soap.assessment: Cholesteatoma of the middle ear/attic with bony scutum erosion.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Refer to Otolaryngology for definitive surgical management via Tympanomastoidectomy (canal wall up or canal wall down technique) to excise the cholesteatoma matrix and prevent recurrence or further erosion. 2. Obtain High-Resolution CT of the temporal bone to map the extent of bony erosion (ossicular chain, tegmen tympani, lateral semicircular canal, facial nerve canal) and screen for complications prior to surgery. 3. Initiate topical antibiotic ear drops (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) and regular aural toilet to control active infection and reduce mucosal edema preoperatively. 4. Arrange long-term post-operative surveillance (otoscopy plus non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI) for recurrent or residual cholesteatoma.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic otoscopic appearance of cholesteatoma (pearly white keratin debris in a retraction pocket of the pars flaccida/attic) and its association with painless, foul-smelling otorrhea and conductive hearing loss
Understand why cholesteatoma requires definitive surgical excision (tympanomastoidectomy) rather than antibiotics alone, given its capacity for progressive bony erosion
Identify red-flag complications of cholesteatoma (labyrinthine fistula/vertigo, facial nerve palsy, intracranial extension) that mandate urgent escalation
Outline the role of high-resolution CT temporal bone imaging in preoperative planning and the need for long-term surveillance for recurrence

teaching.one_liner: An abnormal skin growth in the middle ear from chronic ear disease, slowly eroding surrounding bone and causing painless, foul-smelling drainage and progressive hearing loss — treated surgically, since it can erode into the inner ear or brain if untreated.
differentials: Chronic suppurative otitis media without cholesteatoma
red_flags: Dizziness, facial weakness, or severe headache — could indicate erosion into the inner ear or intracranial spread

must_ask.say: Does the drainage from your ear have a foul smell?
How many months has this drainage been going on?
Has your hearing gotten worse in that ear?
Is there any pain, or is it painless?
Did you have frequent ear infections as a child?
